prompt: Why does every type in Go satisfy `any`?
hint: How many methods does `any` ask for?

choices.text: Each type quietly declares that it implements `any`
choices.why: Go has no `implements` at all; lesson 27 showed satisfaction is decided by the methods a type has.

choices.text: It lists no methods, and every type has all of zero
choices.why: Right. A type satisfies an interface by having its methods, and `any` asks for none.

choices.text: Type checking is switched off for variables declared `any`
choices.why: The compiler checks every use of an `any`; it refused `a + b` in section 03.

choices.text: Each type embeds `any`, the way a class extends a base class
choices.why: Go has no base class to extend. Nothing is embedded; the empty method list is the whole reason.

prompt: After `var v any = 42` and then `v = "Ana"`, what does `fmt.Printf("%T", v)` print?
hint: `%T` reports the type of what is inside.

choices.text: `any`
choices.why: `any` is the variable's own type, which never changes; `%T` prints the type of the value it holds.

choices.text: `string`
choices.why: Right. The dynamic type is whatever was stored last, and that was a string.

choices.text: `int`, the type it was declared with
choices.why: It was declared `any`; 42 was only its first value, and the second replaced it, type and all.

choices.text: `interface {}`
choices.why: That is how `%T` writes `any` itself, as with `*interface {}`; for `v` it names what `v` holds.

prompt: The type of the value stored inside an interface, the one `%T` prints, is called its ___ type.
hint: It can change every time something new is stored.

prompt: On the lab's machine, how many bytes does a variable of type `any` take, whatever it holds?
hint: Two words of 8 bytes: what are they?

prompt: `names` is a `[]string`. Why is `fmt.Println(names...)` refused?
hint: What are the elements of the slice `Println` wants?

choices.text: A slice cannot be passed with `...` to a variadic function
choices.why: It can when the types match: lesson 21 passed `scores...` to `sum(nums ...int)`.

choices.text: `any` does not accept strings
choices.why: It accepts every type; `fmt.Println("ana", "bia")` passes two strings as two `any` values.

choices.text: It needs a `[]any`, whose elements are interface values, and no conversion builds one in place
choices.why: Right. Each string has to go into an interface in a new slice, and Go makes you write that loop.

choices.text: Strings in a slice are not comparable
choices.why: Strings compare fine, and printing compares nothing; the problem is the element type.

prompt: `{"age": 31}` is decoded into a `map[string]any`. What type does `doc["age"]` hold?
hint: JSON has a single kind of number.

choices.text: `int`, since 31 has no decimal point
choices.why: `Unmarshal` does not look at the point; with no struct to ask, every number gets the same type.

choices.text: `float64`
choices.why: Right. The documentation lists it: float64, for JSON numbers.

choices.text: `json.Number`, the number's text
choices.why: Only a decoder told `UseNumber()` keeps numbers that way; `Unmarshal` does not.

choices.text: `int64`, so that large ids fit
choices.why: That would have kept the id whole, and section 02 showed it did not.

prompt: A service sends `{"order": 9007199254740995}`, your program decodes it into a `map[string]any` and sends the order id back. What does the service receive?
hint: Where does 9007199254740995 sit against 2⁵³?

choices.text: The same id, because a `float64` has 64 bits
choices.why: Only 52 of them are fraction, so above 2⁵³ not every whole number exists as a `float64`.

choices.text: Nothing: `Unmarshal` returns an error for a number that does not fit
choices.why: In section 02 the id changed and `err` was nil; no error is raised for rounding.

choices.text: A neighbouring number, and nothing reports an error
choices.why: Right. It is past 2⁵³ and odd, so it was rounded to a `float64` that is a different id.

choices.text: The same id, as large numbers become `json.Number` by themselves
choices.why: Nothing switches on its own: `json.Number` needs `UseNumber()` on a decoder.

prompt: `doc["age"]` holds a `float64`. What happens with `years := doc["age"].(int)`?
hint: Can the compiler see what the map holds?

choices.text: The compiler refuses it, since the value is a `float64`
choices.why: The compiler cannot know what a `map[string]any` will hold when the program runs, so it accepts the line.

choices.text: `years` becomes 31, converted from 31.0
choices.why: An assertion is not a conversion. It checks the type and hands the value over, or fails.

choices.text: It compiles, and panics every time the line runs
choices.why: Right: `interface conversion: interface {} is float64, not int`, on line 18.

choices.text: `years` is 0 and the program carries on
choices.why: This single-result form never answers quietly; the form that does is lesson 29's.

prompt: `var a, b any = 2, 3` and then `fmt.Println(a + b)`. What happens?
hint: Which types is `+` defined for, and could `any` be one?

choices.text: It prints 5
choices.why: The values are ints, but the variables are `any`, and the compiler only sees the variables.

choices.text: It prints 23, joining the two like strings
choices.why: `any` is not turned into text; nothing is added or joined, because nothing compiles.

choices.text: It compiles and panics at run time
choices.why: That is the fate of a wrong assertion. Here no assertion was written and the compiler stops first.

choices.text: The build fails: `+` is not defined on `any`
choices.why: Right: `operator + not defined on a (variable of interface type any)`.

prompt: `x` is a variable of type `any`. Which of these compile without a type assertion? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does every Go value support?

choices.text: `fmt.Println(x)`
choices.why: Yes. `Println` takes `...any`, and passing an `any` is something every value allows.

choices.text: `len(x)`
choices.why: Refused: `invalid argument: s (variable of interface type any) for built-in len`.

choices.text: `x == y`, with `y` another `any`
choices.why: Yes, it compiles; it can still panic at run time if both hold slices.

choices.text: `var n int = x`
choices.why: Refused, and the message names the fix: `need type assertion`.

choices.text: `var y any = x`
choices.why: Yes. Assigning one `any` to another needs nothing.

prompt: `sum(xs []any)` asserts each element to `float64`. Why does `sum([]any{1.5, 2})` panic?
hint: What type does an untyped `2` take when nothing asks for one?

choices.text: The `2` went in as an `int`, its default type
choices.why: Right. An `any` asks for no type, so the constant took its default, and the assertion wanted `float64`.

choices.text: A `float64` cannot hold the number 2 exactly
choices.why: It can: 2 is a small whole number, and `[]float64{1.5, 2}` worked fine in the typed version.

choices.text: A `[]any` cannot mix a float and an int
choices.why: It can mix anything; section 02 put five different types in one `[]any`.

choices.text: `go vet` would have reported it, and nobody ran it
choices.why: It was run, as `go vet && go run .`, and passed: nothing here breaks a rule it knows.

prompt: `var c, d any = 1, 1.0` and then `fmt.Println(c == d)` prints `false`. Why?
hint: Two interface values are equal when two things are equal.

choices.text: `1.0` is stored inexactly, as floats are
choices.why: 1.0 is exact in a `float64`; the comparison never gets as far as the numbers.

choices.text: Two interface values are compared by address, as two separate boxes
choices.why: `a == b` with 1 and 1 printed `true`, so it is not the address that is compared.

choices.text: One holds an `int` and the other a `float64`
choices.why: Right. The dynamic types differ, so the values are never compared.

choices.text: `==` is refused between interfaces and answers false
choices.why: A refusal would be a compile error; `==` on interfaces compiles and compares type and value.

prompt: A cache is a `map[any]bool`. What happens when code runs `seen[key] = true` with `key` an `any` holding `[]int{1, 2}`?
hint: A map has to compare keys; lesson 14 said which types can be keys.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a slice as a map key
choices.why: It would for `map[[]int]bool`. Here the key type is `any`, which is comparable, so it compiles.

choices.text: It compiles, and panics when that line runs
choices.why: Right. Inside an `any` the compiler cannot see the slice; the lab's run printed `hash of unhashable type []int`.

choices.text: It stores the slice's address as the key
choices.why: Go never compares slices by address; a slice is not comparable at all.

choices.text: It stores a copy of the slice, keyed by its contents
choices.why: That is what an array key would give, `[2]int`; a slice cannot be hashed.

prompt: Match each need to the tool section 03 suggests for it.
hint: Behaviour, the same code for several types, and the unknown.

pairs.left: One `Sum` that works for `int` and for `float64`
Every type that can be written to, files and buffers alike
A JSON document whose shape nobody knew in advance
A JSON document whose fields are known

right_distractors: A `[]any` with a conversion for every element

prompt: `var p *Player` and then `var v any = p`. What does `fmt.Println(p == nil, v == nil)` print?
hint: What does `v` hold besides the pointer?

choices.text: `true true`
choices.why: That is the common belief. `v` holds a type, `*main.Player`, so it is not an empty interface.

choices.text: `true false`
choices.why: Right. The pointer is nil; the interface has its type word filled, so it is not.

choices.text: `false false`
choices.why: `p` was declared and never given a value, so it is a nil pointer and `p == nil` is true.

choices.text: No output: comparing an interface with `nil` is refused
choices.why: It compiles; `== nil` is how you ask whether an interface holds no type at all.

prompt: An interface value compares equal to `nil` only when it holds no value and no ___ either.
hint: It is the word that `%T` prints.

prompt: In the first version of `lookup`, there is no `zoe` in the map. What does the loop print for her?
hint: `lookup` returns `p` as an `any`, and the caller tests `r != nil`.

choices.text: `zoe not found`, from the `else` branch
choices.why: That is what the fixed version printed. Here `r != nil` was true, since `r` held a type.

choices.text: `zoe found: <nil>`
choices.why: Right. The test passed, and `%v` printed the nil pointer inside as `<nil>`.

choices.text: Nothing: `lookup` panics on the nil pointer
choices.why: `lookup` only returns the pointer; nothing reads through it until `.Name` on the last line.

choices.text: Nothing: returning a `*Player` as `any` does not compile
choices.why: Every type satisfies `any`, so `return p` compiled, and `go vet` passed too.

prompt: `func open(name string) io.Reader` returns `f`, a `*os.File` variable that stays nil when the file is missing. Callers test `if r := open(n); r != nil`. What is the sound fix?
hint: The same two words as the figure, with `io.Reader` in place of `any`.

choices.text: Test `r != (io.Reader)(nil)` in the callers instead
choices.why: That is the same question as `r != nil`, an empty interface, and it gets the same wrong answer.

choices.text: Return `nil` itself when `f` is nil, or return `*os.File`
choices.why: Right. Either the interface comes back with no type, or the caller compares a pointer with nil.

choices.text: Run `go vet`, which reports a nil pointer stored in an interface
choices.why: `go vet` passed the `lookup` program in silence; nothing about it breaks a rule.

choices.text: Print `r` with `%v` before testing it
choices.why: `%v` prints `<nil>` for both kinds of nil, which is why the bug hides in logs.

prompt: Put in order what happens when the first `lookup("zoe")` runs and its result is tested.
hint: Start inside `find`.
items: `find` returns a nil `*Player`, since the map has no `zoe`
`return p` stores that pointer in the `any`, filling its type word

prompt: Which of these statements about `any` are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sections 02, 03 and 04 each give one.

choices.text: It is an alias for `interface{}`, and arrived in Go 1.18
choices.why: Yes: `go doc builtin.any`, and a `go 1.17` module refused it.

choices.text: Decoding JSON into it turns whole numbers into `int`
choices.why: Every JSON number becomes a `float64`, `31` included.

choices.text: A wrong assertion on it compiles and fails at run time
choices.why: Yes: `.(int)` on a `float64` built and then panicked.

choices.text: A `[]string` can be passed wherever a `[]any` is expected
choices.why: The compiler refused `fmt.Println(names...)`; each string must go into a new `[]any`.

choices.text: Holding a nil pointer, it does not compare equal to `nil`
choices.why: Yes: the type word is filled, so `v == nil` printed `false`.
